## Purpose {.unnumbered .unlisted}

::: {.content-visible when-format="pdf"}
\begin{marginfigure}
\vspace{1em}
\resizebox{\linewidth}{!}{\mlphysicalstackfull{20}{20}{20}{20}{20}}
\end{marginfigure}

_Under what auditable chain of physical evidence is an autonomous machine permitted to move among humans?_

Releasing a machine allows its software to produce physical consequences outside the test environment. That permission requires an argument connecting the intended operation to evidence about the assembled system. Model accuracy alone cannot ensure the machine stops within its clearance, nor can a demonstration confirm the fallback's effectiveness under required faults. The release decision must identify which measurements support each claim and which assumptions limit its scope. A change in payload or operating conditions can invalidate the argument even when the software remains unchanged. Operating authority carries conditions the deployed system must monitor and specify responses when they no longer hold. Release brings the brain's capabilities, the nervous system's enforcement, and the body's measured limits under one accountable judgment about where the machine may operate and what evidence must remain valid for that permission to continue.

{{< pagebreak >}}

::: {.callout-learning-objectives}

- Construct a release argument linking a bounded operating claim to auditable physical evidence
- Evaluate whether evidence supports operation, conditional operation, or refusal within the proposed envelope
- Specify standing conditions that withdraw operating authority when measurements or configuration changes invalidate a release
- Diagnose unsupported assumptions and weak evidence through adversarial review of a release argument

:::

## The Decision to Deploy {#sec-release-decision-to-deploy}

A directory of passing test records and hardware fault traces does not answer the ultimate systems question: under what auditable chain of physical evidence can an autonomous machine move among humans? In enterprise software or web services, deploying a new build carries operational and financial risk—a regression may corrupt a customer database or degrade service latency. In physical AI, the decision to release delegates physical authority over mass, force, and velocity into an unstructured world populated by human beings. An unhandled edge case, a perceptual hallucination, or an unbudgeted compute latency spike does not terminate in a benign software stack trace; it converts stored electrical, chemical, or hydraulic energy into crushing kinetic work against physical structures and human bodies. Even after adversarial verification harnesses have systematically stressed cyber-physical assumptions—injecting clock drift, memory bus contention, sensor resonance spoofing, and hardware fault conditions into target silicon and mechanics—the engineering challenge shifts from uncovering defects to proving bounds. Yet in engineering practice, development teams routinely attempt to justify deployment using ungrounded statistical optimism: quoting 99.9 percent benchmark accuracy on static validation datasets, or showcasing thousands of error-free cycles recorded during controlled laboratory demonstrations. Neither metric addresses the release question. High validation accuracy merely demonstrates that a learned policy can reproduce training correlations under stationary data distributions, while a flawless laboratory demonstration proves only that a single sequence of states executed safely under the particular environmental conditions present during that run. Deciding to deploy is not a statistical prediction; it is an evidence-based engineering adjudication that formalizes whether empirical data bounds the physical risk of operation.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↰ **Prerequisite:** The empirical verification evidence backing release claims is produced in @sec-verification-qualification-ladder.
:::

As illustrated in the architecture stack in @fig-16-locator, Safety Cases and Release Governance form the third pillar of Tier 4 (System Governance & Assurance). Operating at supervisory cadences of $0.1\text{ to }1\text{ Hz}$, release governance serves as the constitutional gatekeeper of the physical AI stack. It does not generate control actions; rather, it evaluates whether the mechanisms constructed and tested across every lower tier cohere into an unbroken, auditable argument:

- **The Brain (Tier 3):** evaluating whether the uninterpretable representations and probabilistic trajectory proposals of vision-language-action policies are bounded by provable constraints;[^fn-bridge-release-brain]
- **The Nervous System (Tier 2):** verifying that independent enforcers, watchdogs, and fallbacks can revoke learned-policy tracking within the deadlines derived for this plant; the worked $1\text{ ms}$ control period is distinct from full stopping response;[^fn-bridge-release-nervous] and
- **The Body (Tier 1):** grounding all safety claims in the hard physics of contact mechanics, effective moving inertia, motor winding thermal limits, and biomechanical human injury thresholds (such as ISO/TS 15066).[^fn-bridge-release-body]

[^fn-bridge-release-brain]: **Privilege Separation in Cognitive Architecture**\index{Privilege separation!Tier 3 release}: As established in @sec-brain-embodied, Tier 3 cognitive models are probabilistic and unverified. Release governance ensures that learned policies are never granted direct actuator authority, requiring all proposed setpoints to pass through deterministic enforcers. Granting direct actuator access to unverified latent representations risks commanding trajectory setpoints that exceed mechanical joint limits or induce destructive high-speed collisions.

[^fn-bridge-release-nervous]: **Enforcement and Safe Sets**\index{Deterministic enforcement!Tier 2 release}: As detailed in @sec-nervous-multi-rate-bridge and @sec-enforcement-safe-sets-conditional-permission, a sampled control barrier can constrain admitted commands under its model, state-estimation, input, and timing assumptions. The release case checks those assumptions and independent preemption under the claimed faults. Bus starvation or software lockups can otherwise consume the stopping margin.

[^fn-bridge-release-body]: **Causal Boundaries and Contact Criteria**\index{Causal boundaries!Tier 1 release}: As analyzed in @sec-boundary-causal-boundary and @sec-body-five-budgets, the contact assessment must name effective moving mass, geometry, stiffness, body region, pressure, and velocity. ISO/TS 15066 supplies body-region-dependent guidance; a handover force criterion is a conservative selection for an assessed contact case, not a universal transient-contact threshold.

The release this chapter works through is the warehouse mobile manipulator's service at one site: driving the aisles past rack ends where a person may be standing, opening the spring-latched cage door, and handing items to the coworker at the packing station. Each job carries its own criterion, a clear distance for the base and a contact force for the arm, and model accuracy establishes none of them. Release therefore depends on pre-contact clearance, measured brake capability, a bounded full response path, and fault evidence.[^fn-bridge-release-verification] An enforcer time measured on an unloaded processor is useful evidence, but neither an unloaded time nor a percentile can serve as the hard response bound.

[^fn-bridge-release-verification]: **Fault Evidence**\index{Fault manifest!Tier 4 release}: @Sec-verification-fault-injection and @sec-verification-fault-manifest describe signed, reproducible fault records. They document responses to injected conditions; a finite campaign does not by itself establish the worst possible response or coverage of untested fault modes.

A release verdict is a bounded, revocable judgment. The chapter builds that judgment from the operating envelope, a claim-argument-evidence tree, three signed verdicts, standing conditions, and a manifest whose invalid evidence withdraws permission.

## The Release Question {#sec-release-question}

The release question is whether evidence justifies a particular machine's motion in a defined operating domain. The argument names the physical bounds, specified fault set, and validated permission and fallback path. It can support a revocable grant of tracking authority while those conditions hold; it cannot infer protection against every possible fault from finite tests (\ref{dfn-release-goal-structured-safety-case}).

::: {#dfn-release-goal-structured-safety-case .callout-definition title="Claim-argument-evidence safety case"}

***Claim-argument-evidence safety case***\index{Claim-argument-evidence safety case!definition}\index{Safety case!physical AI} is the auditable, structured assurance argument for a specified physical machine, operating envelope, hazard criteria, and fault model, linking top-level safety claims to concrete empirical evidence through explicit engineering warrants.

1.  **Significance**: Transforms subjective, informal deployment confidence into an auditable, falsifiable engineering argument that connects high-level safety goals to concrete empirical evidence across the entire physical stack.
2.  **Distinction**: Unlike software unit test suites or static model validation scorecards, a physical safety case explicitly links operational design domain boundaries, hardware fault injection logs, and runtime enforcer tripwires to demonstrate bounded residual risk.
3.  **Common pitfall**: Treating the safety case as a retrospective compliance checklist completed after development, rather than a living architectural contract that governs feature integration and release gating.

:::

```{python}
#| label: calc-release-operating-envelope
#| echo: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ THE MACHINE'S OPERATING ENVELOPE FOR RELEASE
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-release-question (envelope and conditional-zone paragraphs),
# │          @tbl-16-odd-invariants, the contact-criteria paragraph after it, and
# │          the binding-contract paragraphs of @sec-release-three-verdicts.
# │ Goal: Scope the release case to the running machine's operating envelope.
# │ Show: aisle speed and its ceiling, tote-rack payload, the friction bands and
# │       the inspected-floor ceiling, the clear distance, the latch and handover
# │       speeds with their limits, and the slow-downs before a takeover.
# │ How: RM/AISLE fields; ceilings from calc_max_permitted_velocity with a_eff,
# │      the constant deceleration whose distance matches calc_c2_stop_suffix,
# │      and the three overheads; mu_min = a_brake/g.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt, fmt_velocity, fmt_length, fmt_qty, fmt_latency, check
from mlsysim.physics.robotics import calc_max_permitted_velocity, calc_c2_stop_suffix

# ┌── 1. LOAD: the running machine and its site ─────────────────────────────────
RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator
AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle
g_std = (1 * ureg.standard_gravity).to(meter / second**2)  # physical constant (Pint)

def _a_eff(a_peak):
    """Constant deceleration giving the C2 suffix's distance: v^2 / (2 d_C2).

    d_C2 is proportional to v^2 / a, so v^2 / (2 d_C2) = a / 1.5 at any speed;
    evaluating it at aisle speed stays exact where a solver works at another speed.
    """
    d_c2 = calc_c2_stop_suffix(AISLE.v_aisle, a_peak)["distance"]
    return (AISLE.v_aisle**2 / (2 * d_c2)).to(meter / second**2)

# ┌── 2. EXECUTE: ceilings and friction bands ───────────────────────────────────
a_eff = _a_eff(AISLE.a_brake)  # C2 stop suffix as an equivalent constant deceleration
v_ceiling = calc_max_permitted_velocity(AISLE.d_clear, AISLE.tau_delay, a_eff, AISLE.delta_loc + AISLE.eps_track, AISLE.delta_margin).to(
    meter / second
)
mu_min = (AISLE.a_brake / g_std).to("dimensionless").magnitude
a_inspected = min(AISLE.a_brake, (AISLE.mu_inspected_floor * g_std).to(meter / second**2))
v_inspected_ceiling = calc_max_permitted_velocity(
    AISLE.d_clear, AISLE.tau_delay, _a_eff(a_inspected), AISLE.delta_loc + AISLE.eps_track, AISLE.delta_margin
).to(meter / second)
v_handover_ceiling = (AISLE.f_contact_criterion / (AISLE.k_contact_human * RM.arm_effective_contact_mass) ** 0.5).to(meter / second)

# ┌── 3. GUARD: canon values quoted in the prose and the table ──────────────────
check(abs(v_ceiling.magnitude - 1.3898) < 5e-5, "Aisle ceiling is 1.39 m/s")
check(AISLE.v_aisle < v_ceiling, "Chosen aisle speed sits under the ceiling")
check(abs(mu_min - 0.204) < 5e-4, "Friction needed for a_brake is 0.204")
check(abs(v_inspected_ceiling.magnitude - 1.0947) < 5e-5, "Inspected-floor ceiling is 1.09 m/s")
check(abs(v_handover_ceiling.magnitude - 0.1179) < 5e-5, "Handover ceiling is 0.118 m/s")
check(AISLE.v_handover < v_handover_ceiling, "Chosen handover speed sits under its ceiling")
check(abs(RM.loaded_mass.to(kilogram).magnitude - 368.0) < 1e-9, "Loaded mass is 368 kg")
check(AISLE.v_takeover_in_loop < AISLE.v_aisle, "Slow-down before an in-loop takeover")
check(AISLE.mu_oil_film < AISLE.mu_inspected_floor < mu_min < AISLE.mu_dry, "Friction bands are ordered")
check(abs(AISLE.v_aisle.to(meter / second).magnitude - 1.3) < 1e-9, "Signed aisle speed 1.3 m/s")
check(abs(AISLE.d_clear.to(meter).magnitude - 1.10) < 1e-9, "Clear distance 1.10 m")
check(abs(AISLE.v_takeover_in_loop.to(meter / second).magnitude - 1.2) < 1e-9, "In-loop takeover slow-down 1.2 m/s")
check(abs(AISLE.v_takeover_out_of_loop.to(meter / second).magnitude - 0.3) < 1e-9, "Out-of-loop takeover slow-down 0.3 m/s")
check(abs(AISLE.t_tick.to(millisecond).magnitude - 1.0) < 1e-9, "Permission tick 1 ms")
check(abs(RM.onboard_payload_capacity.to(kilogram).magnitude - 50.0) < 1e-9, "Tote-rack capacity 50 kg")
check(
    abs(AISLE.mu_dry - 0.60) < 1e-9 and abs(AISLE.mu_inspected_floor - 0.12) < 1e-9 and abs(AISLE.mu_oil_film - 0.05) < 1e-9,
    "Friction bands 0.60, 0.12, 0.05",
)
check(abs(AISLE.v_latch_approach.to(meter / second).magnitude - 0.03) < 1e-9, "Guarded latch approach 0.03 m/s")
check(abs(AISLE.v_latch_high.to(meter / second).magnitude - 0.10) < 1e-9, "Unsupported latch approach 0.10 m/s")
check(abs(AISLE.f_latch_tripwire.to(newton).magnitude - 15.0) < 1e-9, "Latch tripwire 15 N")
check(abs(AISLE.t_contact_response.to(millisecond).magnitude - 2.0) < 1e-9, "Contact-loop response 2 ms")
check(abs(AISLE.f_latch_limit.to(newton).magnitude - 100.0) < 1e-9, "Latch limit 100 N")
check(abs(AISLE.v_handover.to(meter / second).magnitude - 0.10) < 1e-9, "Handover speed 0.10 m/s")
check(abs(AISLE.f_contact_criterion.to(newton).magnitude - 50.0) < 1e-9, "Handover criterion 50 N")

# ┌── 4. OUTPUT: rendered values ────────────────────────────────────────────────
class ReleaseEnvelope:
    v_aisle_str = fmt_velocity(AISLE.v_aisle, unit=meter / second, precision=1)
    v_ceiling_str = fmt_velocity(round(v_ceiling.magnitude, 2) * meter / second, unit=meter / second, precision=2)
    v_takeover_in_str = fmt_velocity(AISLE.v_takeover_in_loop, unit=meter / second, precision=1)
    v_takeover_out_str = fmt_velocity(AISLE.v_takeover_out_of_loop, unit=meter / second, precision=1)
    t_tick_str = fmt_latency(AISLE.t_tick, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    payload_str = fmt_qty(RM.onboard_payload_capacity, kilogram, precision=0)
    m1_str = fmt_qty(RM.loaded_mass, kilogram, precision=0)
    mu_min_str = fmt(round(mu_min, 3), precision=3)
    mu_dry_str = fmt(AISLE.mu_dry, precision=2)
    mu_inspected_str = fmt(AISLE.mu_inspected_floor, precision=2)
    mu_oil_str = fmt(AISLE.mu_oil_film, precision=2)
    v_inspected_ceiling_str = fmt_velocity(round(v_inspected_ceiling.magnitude, 2) * meter / second, unit=meter / second, precision=2)
    d_clear_str = fmt_length(AISLE.d_clear, unit=meter, precision=2)
    v_latch_str = fmt_velocity(AISLE.v_latch_approach, unit=meter / second, precision=2)
    v_latch_high_str = fmt_velocity(AISLE.v_latch_high, unit=meter / second, precision=2)
    f_trip_str = fmt_qty(AISLE.f_latch_tripwire, newton, precision=0)
    t_contact_str = fmt_latency(AISLE.t_contact_response, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    f_latch_limit_str = fmt_qty(AISLE.f_latch_limit, newton, precision=0)
    v_handover_str = fmt_velocity(AISLE.v_handover, unit=meter / second, precision=2)
    v_handover_ceiling_str = fmt_velocity(round(v_handover_ceiling.magnitude, 3) * meter / second, unit=meter / second, precision=3)
    f_contact_str = fmt_qty(AISLE.f_contact_criterion, newton, precision=0)
```

A release case is scoped by the operating envelope, the target ODD paired with the machine's own internal conditions. An `UNCOND` verdict authorizes the whole operating envelope (@sec-verification-operating-envelope), a `COND` verdict a named part of it, and `REFUSE` none.\index{Operational design domain!release verdicts} For the mobile manipulator, the operating envelope admits aisle travel at up to `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.v_aisle_str` (chosen; see the Reader Guide) with the tote rack loaded to at most `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.payload_str`, on floors surveyed to a friction coefficient of at least `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.mu_min_str`, past rack ends with at least `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.d_clear_str` of clear distance. It admits door approaches at `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.v_latch_str` and handovers at `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.v_handover_str`. Parts of those ranges are conditional rather than nominal, as specified in @tbl-16-odd-invariants. Unknown measurements do not establish envelope membership.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↰ **Prerequisite:** The operational design domain and its known absences are defined in @sec-data-policy-coverage.
:::

Inside these boundaries the learned policy may propose actions across the nominal task envelope, but each action still requires independent permission. Conditional zones restrict that envelope; for example, the machine slows to `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.v_takeover_in_str` before it requests an in-loop takeover, and on a floor known only through the site's inspection regime it stays below the `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.v_inspected_ceiling_str` inspected-floor ceiling. Unknown measurements and states outside the signed envelope refuse autonomous motion and invoke the separately validated, state-dependent stop.

As formalized in @tbl-16-odd-invariants, each monitored dimension is partitioned into nominal, conditional, and refusal states. The rows are the machine's illustrative configuration; rates, trip response, and stop feasibility require validation on the assembled plant. A conditional state restricts admitted proposals. A refusal state withdraws tracking permission and selects a validated fallback; cutting torque alone can allow a moving load to coast.

\Needspace{28\baselineskip}

| Envelope Dimension / Invariant | Nominal Envelope ($\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{nom}}$)                                                                           | Degraded Boundary ($\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{cond}}$)                                                                                                        | Hard Refusal ($\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{refuse}}$)                                                                                                                         | Runtime Monitor & Rate                                                                 | Enforcer Action & Latency                                                      |
|:-------------------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:-------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Aisle Speed**                | $v\le$ `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.v_aisle_str`                                                                             | `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.v_takeover_in_str` before an in-loop takeover request; `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.v_takeover_out_str` before an out-of-loop one | Measured speed above the signed `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.v_aisle_str` (ceiling `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.v_ceiling_str`), or invalid speed estimate                   | Encoders and IMU, every `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.t_tick_str` permission tick          | Clamp admitted speed; refuse above the signed speed                            |
| **Floor Friction**             | Surveyed $\mu\ge$ `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.mu_min_str` (dry concrete near `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.mu_dry_str`)         | Inspection regime only ($\mu\ge$ `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.mu_inspected_str`): below the `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.v_inspected_ceiling_str` ceiling      | Unsurveyed floor or reported film; a clear oil film ($\mu\approx$ `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.mu_oil_str`) is invisible to the cameras                                   | Floor survey and site spill procedure; no on-board measurement                         | Restrict speed by floor zone; refuse the aisle                                 |
| **Tote-Rack Payload**          | $0\le m\le$ `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.payload_str`, valid load estimate (total at most `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.m1_str`) | Estimate stale since the last pick: stationary arm tasks only                                                                                            | Load above capacity or invalid estimate                                                                                                                                | Rack load cells, at each pick                                                          | Refuse aisle transit until re-weighed                                          |
| **Rack-End Clearance**         | Surveyed $D_{\text{clear}}\ge$ `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.d_clear_str` at every rack end                                   | Shorter surveyed clearance: lower signed speed from the same budget                                                                                      | Unsurveyed rack end, or obstacle inside the clear distance                                                                                                             | Site survey; lidar and navigation camera at frame rate                                 | Speed limit per rack end; stop for a detected obstacle                         |
| **Door Latch Approach**        | $v\le$ `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.v_latch_str`, strike plate at its nominal position                                       | None; demonstrations cover no other latch condition                                                                                                      | `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.v_latch_high_str` approach or displaced plate                                                                                                | Arm contact-force sensing in the `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.t_contact_str` contact loop | Trip at `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.f_trip_str`; refuse the unsupported approach |
| **Coworker Handover**          | TCP speed $\le$ `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.v_handover_str` under `accept_item`                                             | Coworker present without `accept_item`: hold short of the handover point                                                                                 | TCP speed above the signed `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.v_handover_str` (ceiling `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.v_handover_ceiling_str`), or contact outside the assessed case | Joint encoders every permission tick; arm contact-force sensing                        | Clamp TCP speed; refuse above the signed speed                                 |

: **Operating envelope of the warehouse mobile manipulator**: Each listed dimension has disjoint nominal, conditional, and refusal intervals. Conditional operation requires every dimension to remain in a signed admissible interval; missing or invalid measurements refuse. Sensor rates and stopping response are plant validation obligations. {#tbl-16-odd-invariants tbl-colwidths="[16,16,18,18,16,16]"}

A defensible release claim states its plant, contact geometry, and fault set.[^fn-std-isots15066-biomech] The machine's case uses three criteria. The base stops inside the `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.d_clear_str` clear distance before it reaches a person who has stepped out at a rack end, the arm opens the door without exceeding the `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.f_latch_limit_str` latch limit, and a handover never presses on the coworker with more than a chosen `{python} ReleaseEnvelope.f_contact_str` peak force for an assessed contact case. The base's claim protects a person who has stepped out and stands still; a person still walking toward the machine is a separate premise, carried by a site crossing rule (@sec-memory-belief-through-occlusion). The release argument must demonstrate which human contacts are excluded before impact, which detected contacts the model covers, and which single faults the independent fallback handles. A stop after contact does not by itself cap the first force peak.[^fn-math-contact-mechanics]

[^fn-std-isots15066-biomech]: **ISO/TS 15066 Biomechanical Limits**\index{ISO/TS 15066!biomechanical limits}: The specification gives body-region- and contact-type-dependent force and pressure data [@isots15066]. A site assessment must select the applicable body region, contact geometry, and measurement procedure. The handover criterion used here is a conservative case criterion, not a universal ISO/TS 15066 threshold or an injury boundary.

[^fn-math-contact-mechanics]: **Contact Mechanics Force Model**\index{Contact mechanics!force model}: The elastodynamic model couples translational kinetic energy, effective moving inertia, and contact interface stiffness to determine transient peak impact force during an unmitigated collision. Impacting a rigid boundary concentrates stored kinetic energy into a sub-millisecond impulse with severe force amplification, whereas elastic compliance extends deformation time and dissipates energy over a longer stroke. For the formal elastodynamic derivation and unilateral contact formulations, see @sec-appendix-control-contact.

```{python}
#| label: calc-release-biomechanical-impact-envelope
#| echo: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ HANDOVER CONTACT FORCE AND THE BASE'S STOPPING SPARE
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-release-question, @eq-release-unbraked-force and the two
# │          paragraphs after it.
# │ Goal: Show why the arm's handover speed is capped, and how little input
# │       error the base's finished budget can absorb at aisle speed.
# │ Show: unbraked force at the free-space TCP limit and at the handover speed;
# │       budget and spare at 1.3 m/s; the delay and the deceleration shortfall
# │       that each consume the spare.
# │ How: calc_transient_impact_force with the arm's effective contact mass and
# │      the coworker tissue stiffness; calc_safe_stopping_distance with a_eff,
# │      the constant deceleration whose distance matches calc_c2_stop_suffix,
# │      and the three overheads.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_qty, fmt_multiple, fmt_latency, fmt_acceleration, fmt_length, fmt_velocity, fmt_percent, fmt_sci_qty, check
from mlsysim.physics.robotics import calc_safe_stopping_distance, calc_transient_impact_force, calc_c2_stop_suffix

# ┌── 1. LOAD: the running machine and its site ─────────────────────────────────
RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator
AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle

def _a_eff(a_peak):
    """Constant deceleration giving the C2 suffix's distance: v^2 / (2 d_C2).

    d_C2 is proportional to v^2 / a, so v^2 / (2 d_C2) = a / 1.5 at any speed;
    evaluating it at aisle speed stays exact where a solver works at another speed.
    """
    d_c2 = calc_c2_stop_suffix(AISLE.v_aisle, a_peak)["distance"]
    return (AISLE.v_aisle**2 / (2 * d_c2)).to(meter / second**2)

# ┌── 2. EXECUTE: contact forces, then the budget at aisle speed ────────────────
m_eff = RM.arm_effective_contact_mass
f_at_tcp_limit = calc_transient_impact_force(RM.tcp_speed_limit, m_eff, AISLE.k_contact_human).to(newton)
f_ratio = (f_at_tcp_limit / AISLE.f_contact_criterion).to("dimensionless").magnitude
f_at_handover = calc_transient_impact_force(AISLE.v_handover, m_eff, AISLE.k_contact_human).to(newton)
v_handover_ceiling = (AISLE.f_contact_criterion / (AISLE.k_contact_human * m_eff) ** 0.5).to(meter / second)

c2_braking = calc_c2_stop_suffix(AISLE.v_aisle, AISLE.a_brake)["distance"].to(meter)
a_eff = _a_eff(AISLE.a_brake)  # C2 stop suffix as an equivalent constant deceleration
overhead_loc = AISLE.delta_loc + AISLE.eps_track
budget_aisle = calc_safe_stopping_distance(AISLE.v_aisle, AISLE.tau_delay, a_eff, overhead_loc, AISLE.delta_margin).to(millimeter)
spare_aisle = (AISLE.d_clear - budget_aisle).to(millimeter)
t_spare = (spare_aisle / AISLE.v_aisle).to(millisecond)
# Deceleration at which the budget exactly fills the clear distance. The C2
# braking distance scales as 1/a, so a' = a_brake * d_C2(a_brake) / room.
braking_room = (AISLE.d_clear - AISLE.v_aisle * AISLE.tau_delay - overhead_loc - AISLE.delta_margin).to(meter)
a_break_even = (AISLE.a_brake * c2_braking / braking_room).to(meter / second**2)
a_shortfall_pct = ((AISLE.a_brake - a_break_even) / AISLE.a_brake).to("dimensionless").magnitude * 100.0

# ┌── 3. GUARD: canon values quoted in the prose ────────────────────────────────
check(abs(m_eff.to(kilogram).magnitude - 12.0) < 1e-9, "Effective contact mass is 12.0 kg")
check(abs(f_at_tcp_limit.magnitude - 424.26) < 0.01, "Unbraked force at the TCP limit")
check(abs(f_ratio - 8.49) < 0.01, "About 8.5x the 50 N criterion")
check(abs(f_at_handover.magnitude - 42.43) < 0.01, "Handover force is 42.4 N")
check(abs(v_handover_ceiling.magnitude - 0.1179) < 5e-5, "Handover ceiling is 0.118 m/s")
check(AISLE.v_handover < v_handover_ceiling, "Chosen handover speed sits under its ceiling")
check(abs(budget_aisle.magnitude - 997.43) < 5e-3, "Finished budget at 1.3 m/s")
check(abs(spare_aisle.magnitude - 102.57) < 5e-3, "Spare at 1.3 m/s")
check(abs(t_spare.magnitude - 78.9) < 0.05, "Spare spent as delay is 78.9 ms")
check(abs(a_shortfall_pct - 13.9) < 0.1, "A 14 percent deceleration shortfall fills the spare")

# ┌── 4. OUTPUT: rendered values ────────────────────────────────────────────────
class BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope:
    m_eff_str = fmt_qty(m_eff, kilogram, precision=0)
    v_tcp_str = fmt_velocity(RM.tcp_speed_limit, unit=meter / second, precision=0)
    k_h_str = fmt_qty(AISLE.k_contact_human, newton / meter, precision=0, commas=True)
    f_tcp_str = fmt_qty(round(f_at_tcp_limit.magnitude) * newton, newton, precision=0)
    f_ratio_mult_str = fmt_multiple(f_ratio, precision=1)
    f_limit_str = fmt_qty(AISLE.f_contact_criterion, newton, precision=0)
    v_handover_str = fmt_velocity(AISLE.v_handover, unit=meter / second, precision=2)
    f_handover_str = fmt_qty(f_at_handover, newton, precision=1)
    v_handover_ceiling_str = fmt_velocity(round(v_handover_ceiling.magnitude, 3) * meter / second, unit=meter / second, precision=3)
    v_aisle_str = fmt_velocity(AISLE.v_aisle, unit=meter / second, precision=1)
    d_clear_str = fmt_length(AISLE.d_clear, unit=meter, precision=2)
    budget_str = fmt_length(round(budget_aisle.magnitude, 1) * millimeter, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    spare_str = fmt_length(round(spare_aisle.magnitude, 1) * millimeter, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    t_spare_str = fmt_latency(round(t_spare.magnitude, 1) * millisecond, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    a_brake_str = fmt_acceleration(AISLE.a_brake, unit=meter / second**2, precision=0)
    a_shortfall_pct_str = fmt_percent(round(a_shortfall_pct) / 100.0, precision=0, style="prose")
```

Consider the arm at its free-space speed limit of `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.v_tcp_str`, with a robot-side effective mass at the tool center point of `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.m_eff_str`. In an unbraked elastic contact with the coworker's hand, modeled with an effective tissue stiffness $k_h$ of `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.k_h_str`, the peak contact force follows @eq-release-unbraked-force:
$$F_{\text{unbraked}} = v\,\sqrt{k_h\,m_{\text{eff}}}$$ {#eq-release-unbraked-force}
At the free-space limit this ideal elastic model predicts `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.f_tcp_str`, or `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.f_ratio_mult_str` the chosen `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.f_limit_str` criterion, so the arm cannot enter an unseparated contact at that speed without a stronger, measured protection argument. The same equation sets the handover speed, since the criterion admits at most `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.v_handover_ceiling_str`. At the chosen `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.v_handover_str`, the model predicts `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.f_handover_str`, inside the criterion (@sec-intervention-human-authority).

The base's claim is a budget rather than a single force. Stopping distance grows linearly with the delay before braking and quadratically with speed (@eq-enforce-stopping-envelope), and the delay components this chapter must evidence are the lease path and the observation age that its claims name. At the `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.v_aisle_str` aisle speed, the finished budget of @sec-enforcement-stopping-envelopes is `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.budget_str` against the `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.d_clear_str` clear distance, a spare of `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.spare_str`. That spare is the whole allowance for error in the budget's inputs. An unbudgeted delay of `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.t_spare_str` spends it, and so does a loaded deceleration `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.a_shortfall_pct_str` below the `{python} BiomechanicalImpactEnvelope.a_brake_str` the budget assumes. Whatever the person's position inside the clear distance, a stopping claim whose inputs are unmeasured cannot show that its spare survives them (\ref{chk-release-contact-force-and-stopping-envelope-budget}).

::: {#chk-release-contact-force-and-stopping-envelope-budget .callout-checkpoint title="Biomechanical force and stopping distance"}

Before signing off on human-robot coexistence envelopes, verify your understanding of biomechanical impact forces, delay, and braking clearance:

- [ ] **Biomechanical injury thresholds**: Can you explain why the arm's unbraked contact at its free-space speed exceeds the handover criterion by nearly an order of magnitude, and how the same model sets the handover speed?
- [ ] **Reaction drift vs. active braking**: Can you distinguish between the linear reaction displacement during the pre-brake delay and the quadratic dissipation of kinetic energy during active braking?
- [ ] **Spare and input error**: Can you describe how an unbudgeted delay or a shortfall in credible deceleration spends the budget's spare and invalidates a release claim?
:::

Accountability for the release decision must reside with an identifiable **lead systems adjudicator**\index{Lead systems adjudicator!accountability} rather than being diffused across development teams. In complex physical AI architectures, diffusion of responsibility is a primary organizational failure mode. A vision team signs off on mean average precision scores, an actuator supplier signs off on motor torque curves, and a reinforcement learning team signs off on policy convergence. Each group assumes that another layer provides the margin of safety. The lead systems adjudicator alone assumes personal technical authority for the release verdict, attesting that the integrated system satisfies the safety case. This attestation binds the verdict to a set of immutable technical artifacts, including the cryptographic hash of the verified policy weights, the calibration logs of the arm's contact-force sensing, the brake-onset trials together with a separately justified worst-response bound, and the stopping trials at the loaded mass that establish the credible deceleration. Signing records the adjudicator's bounded judgment about that evidence and the specified operating domain.

Every release verdict carries an expiration boundary defined by physical degradation and environmental change. A machine whose release case was accepted at commissioning can become unsafe through operational drift, out-of-distribution physical interactions, and unmodeled mechanical wear. Over months of warehouse operation, calibration drift in the arm's contact-force sensing erodes the resolution that the latch and handover claims rely on, traffic polishes and soils the aisle floor that the braking claim assumes, ambient temperature swings alter motor coil resistance (as established in @sec-body-five-budgets), and gear backlash in the arm joints increases tracking errors while degrading braking efficiency. Out-of-distribution interactions, such as a coworker presenting an item with unfamiliar surface compliance, invalidate the momentum transfer assumptions of the contact proof. When sensor diagnostics detect parameter drift beyond tolerance, or when total operating cycles reach the service limit of the mechanical friction brakes, the **release verdict**\index{Release verdict!invalidation} is invalidated automatically. The release question must then be asked again, demanding a renewed chain of evidence before physical authority can be restored.

## Safety Cases and Claims {#sec-release-safety-cases-claims}

A safety case is a structured argument that a physical machine meets its safety claims within a specified operating envelope. Adapting Stephen Toulmin's structural argumentation framework [@toulmin1958uses], Goal Structuring Notation (GSN)\index{Goal Structuring Notation}[^fn-std-gsn-argument] [@kelly1998arguing; @kelly2004goal], and the UL 4600 autonomy evaluation standard [@koopman2020how], this argument takes the form of a **claim-argument-evidence (CAE) safety case**\index{Claim-argument-evidence safety case!argument structure}. This framework decomposes a top-level safety proposition (e.g., non-injurious kinetic force dissipation) into falsifiable sub-claims, linking them through architectural and inductive warrants to empirical measurements, hardware logs, and containment proofs.

[^fn-std-gsn-argument]: **Goal Structuring Notation**\index{Goal Structuring Notation!argumentation grammar}: Developed by Tim Kelly at the University of York, GSN provides an explicit graphical grammar for structuring and auditing safety assurance cases [@kelly1998arguing; @kelly2004goal]. The notation decomposes top-level system safety goals into contextual sub-claims, argumentation strategies, and verifiable solutions grounded in empirical test artifacts. Omitting rigorous hierarchical decomposition conceals unverified inductive leaps between high-level policies and low-level physical dynamics.

The root of the tree is the top-level claim, which asserts a measurable physical property required to prevent harm, such as guaranteeing that the loaded base comes to rest before it reaches a person who has stepped out at a rack end, or, for a far heavier machine such as the haul truck in @fig-16-real-autonomous-haul-truck, that its moving mass comes to rest within corridor containment. This top-level claim cannot be validated directly by inspection. Instead, it is broken down through strategies or intermediate arguments that partition the verification problem across operational sub-regimes, physical hazard classes, or architectural subsystems. Each sub-claim terminates either in supporting sub-claims or in concrete evidentiary artifacts, bounded by explicit context and assumptions that define the physical conditions under which the links hold.

::: {#fig-16-real-autonomous-haul-truck fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**Large-machine context**: A loaded Caterpillar 785C haul truck at the Kosse lignite mine illustrates the mass and clearance a release case may need to address. The photograph does not establish autonomous operation, sensing, or braking performance. Photo: Roy Luck, [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Caterpillar_haul_truck,_Luminant_Energy_Kosse_lignite_mine_(5556779421).jpg) ([CC BY 2.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/2.0/)); [original on Flickr](https://www.flickr.com/photos/royluck/5556779421/)." fig-alt="A large yellow Caterpillar 785C truck carries a heaped load of earth on an open mine road. Tall tires and a stairway beside the cab show its scale; dust trails from the rear. Its control mode and braking behavior are not visible."}
![](images/jpg/fig16_real_autonomous_haul_truck.jpg){width="85%" fig-alt="A large yellow Caterpillar 785C truck carries a heaped load of earth on an open mine road. Tall tires and a stairway beside the cab show its scale; dust trails from the rear. Its control mode and braking behavior are not visible."}
:::

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/spa_locator_core.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="S·P·A locator triad highlighting the central causal core."}

*Release assurance: structured safety cases bounding the complete operational envelope across Sense, Plan, and Act.*
:::

The structure's validity hinges on distinguishing genuine evidence from demonstration. A **demonstration**\index{Demonstration!versus evidence} is a record of successful task execution over an uncharacterized test distribution, such as recording ten thousand error-free bin-picking cycles under nominal factory conditions. Demonstrations measure mean performance but do not bound tail behavior or reveal failure modes outside the sampled trajectory. Genuine evidence consists of falsifiable, calibrated artifacts with quantified bounds. In a physical AI system, evidence comprises worst-case timing distributions from real-time hardware execution traces (including stator delays characterized in @sec-body-five-budgets), calibrated sensor noise profiles under degraded environmental states, dynamic load cell measurements recorded across deceleration regimes, and targeted fault injection trials that deliberately force the policy to the boundary of its training distribution. An evidentiary artifact lacking quantified uncertainty or failing to test the physical boundary remains a demonstration and cannot support an inferential link.

Connecting an item of evidence to a claim requires a **warrant**\index{Warrant!inferential rule}, which is the inferential rule stating why the data proves the assertion. In software systems governed by learned policies, this link is inductive, asserting that because the system avoided failure across finite test episodes, it will continue to avoid failure during future deployment. In physical systems operating in continuous state spaces, this inductive link is fundamentally incomplete without a deterministic enforcer.

The exposure wall of @sec-evaluation-trial-limits shows why that inductive link cannot carry a high-consequence claim alone. A zero-event test campaign cannot reach the hazard rates such claims name within any practical schedule, on one machine or a fleet. The argument must therefore add an architectural warrant, grounding the claim in an independent permission path (@sec-enforcement) that bounds actuator torque and withdraws motion whenever a learned command leaves the admitted set. That warrant narrows the claim rather than escaping the wall, since a shield changes the claim only for the hazards it detects and stops in time (@sec-frontier-method-limits).

```{python}
#| label: calc-release-low-light-age
#| echo: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ AN UNSTATED LIGHTING ASSUMPTION IN THE STOPPING BUDGET
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-release-safety-cases-claims (contextual-assumptions paragraph)
# │          and the unstated-assumption pitfall of @sec-release-fallacies-pitfalls.
# │ Goal: Show how a lighting change the budget never named ages the navigation
# │       camera's image and eats into the aisle budget's spare.
# │ Show: nominal and low-light exposure, the added observation age, the added
# │       travel at aisle speed, and its share of the spare.
# │ How: perception age is timed from mid-exposure (AISLE.perception_age), so a
# │      longer exposure adds half its increase; spare from
# │      calc_safe_stopping_distance with a_eff, the constant deceleration
# │      whose distance matches calc_c2_stop_suffix.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_latency, fmt_length, fmt_velocity, fmt_percent, check
from mlsysim.physics.robotics import calc_safe_stopping_distance, calc_c2_stop_suffix

# ┌── 1. LOAD: the running machine, plus one chapter-local input ────────────────
RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator
AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle
low_light_exposure_factor = 2.0  # scenario assumption: dim aisle doubles the exposure

def _a_eff(a_peak):
    """Constant deceleration giving the C2 suffix's distance: v^2 / (2 d_C2).

    d_C2 is proportional to v^2 / a, so v^2 / (2 d_C2) = a / 1.5 at any speed;
    evaluating it at aisle speed stays exact where a solver works at another speed.
    """
    d_c2 = calc_c2_stop_suffix(AISLE.v_aisle, a_peak)["distance"]
    return (AISLE.v_aisle**2 / (2 * d_c2)).to(meter / second**2)

# ┌── 2. EXECUTE ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
t_exp_nominal = RM.nav_camera.exposure_time.to(millisecond)
t_exp_low = (low_light_exposure_factor * t_exp_nominal).to(millisecond)
dt_age = ((t_exp_low - t_exp_nominal) / 2).to(millisecond)  # mid-exposure timestamp
d_added = (AISLE.v_aisle * dt_age).to(millimeter)
a_eff = _a_eff(AISLE.a_brake)  # C2 stop suffix as an equivalent constant deceleration
budget = calc_safe_stopping_distance(AISLE.v_aisle, AISLE.tau_delay, a_eff, AISLE.delta_loc + AISLE.eps_track, AISLE.delta_margin).to(millimeter)
spare = (AISLE.d_clear - budget).to(millimeter)
share_of_spare = (d_added / spare).to("dimensionless").magnitude

# ┌── 3. GUARD ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
check(abs(t_exp_nominal.magnitude - 16.0) < 1e-9, "Navigation-camera exposure 16 ms")
check(abs(dt_age.magnitude - 8.0) < 1e-9, "Low light adds 8 ms of observation age")
check(abs(d_added.magnitude - 10.4) < 1e-9, "10.4 mm of added travel at 1.3 m/s")
check(abs(spare.magnitude - 102.57) < 5e-3, "Spare at 1.3 m/s")
check(abs(share_of_spare - 0.101) < 5e-3, "About a tenth of the spare")

# ┌── 4. OUTPUT ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
class ReleaseLowLight:
    t_exp_nominal_str = fmt_latency(t_exp_nominal, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_exp_low_str = fmt_latency(t_exp_low, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    dt_age_str = fmt_latency(dt_age, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    v_aisle_str = fmt_velocity(AISLE.v_aisle, unit=meter / second, precision=1)
    d_added_str = fmt_length(d_added, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    spare_str = fmt_length(round(spare.magnitude, 1) * millimeter, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    share_str = fmt_percent(round(share_of_spare * 100) / 100.0, precision=0, style="prose")
```

Every argument link relies on contextual assumptions, with unstated assumptions posing the greatest vulnerability in a safety case. A warrant that derives safe stopping distance from measured optical camera frame rates implicitly assumes that ambient illumination remains above the sensor noise threshold, that lens covers remain free from airborne grease, that SerDes (serializer/deserializer) delivery remains within its measured loss and delay budget, and that internal bus arbitration introduces negligible jitter. In a constructed low-light mode, the navigation camera's exposure doubles from `{python} ReleaseLowLight.t_exp_nominal_str` to `{python} ReleaseLowLight.t_exp_low_str`. Because an image's age is timed from mid-exposure, each observation reaches the proposer `{python} ReleaseLowLight.dt_age_str` older, and at the `{python} ReleaseLowLight.v_aisle_str` aisle speed the base travels another `{python} ReleaseLowLight.d_added_str` before the braking command can be issued, about `{python} ReleaseLowLight.share_str` of the budget's `{python} ReleaseLowLight.spare_str` spare. The link between the vision benchmark and the stopping distance claim breaks silently because the physical environment drifted across an unstated boundary. A sound argument explicitly defines every physical dependency as a bounded context element linked to runtime diagnostic monitors that detect assumption violations.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↳ **Downstream:** Epistemic assumptions embedded within safety case warrants are critically interrogated in @sec-frontier-epistemic-limits.
:::

The weakest link governs every claim-argument-evidence tree. A safety case is not an aggregate metric where statistical over-performance in one branch compensates for evidentiary deficits in another. High accuracy on object recognition benchmarks does not offset an uncharacterized $P_{99.9}$ latency spike in the CAN bus transceiver, nor does extensive policy simulation offset the absence of physical dynamometer brake wear data. If a top-level claim decomposes into sub-claims for kinetic energy dissipation, thermal limit protection (e.g., bounding $I^2R$ Joule heating below stator thermal derating limits established in @sec-body-thermal-duty-cycles), and SE(3) trajectory bounding, a failure in the evidence or warrant of any single branch invalidates the root claim. When an adjudicator examines the tree, the goal is not to count the number of supporting artifacts, but to identify the single weakest link whose failure would permit physical damage. Evaluating whether every branch maintains an unbroken chain of evidence from physical measurements to verified limits determines the verdict that governs machine release.

### Match the safety argument to the machine

```{python}
#| label: calc-release-claims
#| echo: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ THE SIX RELEASE CLAIMS ON THE RUNNING MACHINE
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-release-safety-cases-claims (standards paragraph, scorecard
# │          lead-in) and @tbl-16-cae-scorecard.
# │ Goal: Instance claims C1-C6 on the warehouse mobile manipulator.
# │ Show: base budget at aisle speed against the clear distance; latch force at
# │       brake command, remaining compression, and the arm stop it requires;
# │       handover force; renewal-to-onset time; enforcer WCET and deadline;
# │       friction needed for a_brake; observation age; handover fallback time.
# │ How: RM/AISLE fields; calc_safe_stopping_distance with the calc_c2_stop_suffix
# │      distance as an equivalent constant deceleration;
# │      calc_tripwire_contact_force_accumulation; calc_transient_impact_force.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt, fmt_qty, fmt_latency, fmt_acceleration, fmt_length, fmt_velocity, check
from mlsysim.physics.robotics import (
    calc_safe_stopping_distance,
    calc_tripwire_contact_force_accumulation,
    calc_transient_impact_force,
    calc_c2_stop_suffix,
)

# ┌── 1. LOAD: the running machine and its site ─────────────────────────────────
RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator
AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle
g_std = (1 * ureg.standard_gravity).to(meter / second**2)  # physical constant (Pint)

def _a_eff(a_peak):
    """Constant deceleration giving the C2 suffix's distance: v^2 / (2 d_C2).

    d_C2 is proportional to v^2 / a, so v^2 / (2 d_C2) = a / 1.5 at any speed;
    evaluating it at aisle speed stays exact where a solver works at another speed.
    """
    d_c2 = calc_c2_stop_suffix(AISLE.v_aisle, a_peak)["distance"]
    return (AISLE.v_aisle**2 / (2 * d_c2)).to(meter / second**2)

# ┌── 2. EXECUTE: one warrant quantity per claim ────────────────────────────────
# C1 base: finished budget at aisle speed.
a_eff = _a_eff(AISLE.a_brake)  # C2 stop suffix as an equivalent constant deceleration
budget_aisle = calc_safe_stopping_distance(AISLE.v_aisle, AISLE.tau_delay, a_eff, AISLE.delta_loc + AISLE.eps_track, AISLE.delta_margin).to(
    millimeter
)
spare_aisle = (AISLE.d_clear - budget_aisle).to(millimeter)
# C1 door: force at brake command and the arm stop that keeps it under the limit.
f_cmd = calc_tripwire_contact_force_accumulation(AISLE.f_latch_tripwire, AISLE.k_latch, AISLE.v_latch_approach, AISLE.t_contact_response).to(newton)
x_remaining = ((AISLE.f_latch_limit - f_cmd) / AISLE.k_latch).to(millimeter)
a_arm_needed = (AISLE.v_latch_approach**2 / (2 * x_remaining)).to(meter / second**2)
# C1 handover: unbraked elastic force at the handover speed.
f_handover = calc_transient_impact_force(AISLE.v_handover, RM.arm_effective_contact_mass, AISLE.k_contact_human).to(newton)
# C2: last valid renewal to brake onset.
t_renewal_to_onset = (AISLE.t_lease + AISLE.t_tick + AISLE.t_bus + AISLE.t_brake_onset).to(millisecond)
# C3: friction the credible deceleration needs.
mu_min = (AISLE.a_brake / g_std).to("dimensionless").magnitude
# C6: an unacknowledged handover falls back by the spare spent as time.
t_timeout = (spare_aisle / AISLE.v_aisle).to(millisecond)

# ┌── 3. GUARD: canon values quoted in the table ────────────────────────────────
check(abs(budget_aisle.magnitude - 997.43) < 5e-3, "C1 base budget at 1.3 m/s")
check(budget_aisle < AISLE.d_clear, "C1 budget fits inside the clear distance")
check(abs(f_cmd.magnitude - 39.0) < 1e-9, "C1 latch force at brake command")
check(abs(x_remaining.magnitude - 0.1525) < 1e-6, "C1 remaining compression 0.15 mm")
check(abs(a_arm_needed.magnitude - 2.95) < 0.005, "C1 arm stop premise about 3 m/s^2 (computed 2.95)")
check(abs(f_handover.magnitude - 42.43) < 0.01, "C1 handover force 42.4 N")
check(f_handover < AISLE.f_contact_criterion, "C1 handover force under the criterion")
check(abs(t_renewal_to_onset.magnitude - 82.0) < 1e-9, "C2 renewal-to-onset 82 ms")
check(AISLE.enforcer_wcet < AISLE.enforcer_deadline < AISLE.t_tick, "C2 WCET < deadline < tick")
check(abs(mu_min - 0.204) < 5e-4, "C3 friction floor 0.204")
check(abs(AISLE.perception_age.to(millisecond).magnitude - 51.6) < 1e-9, "C4 age 51.6 ms")
check(abs(t_timeout.magnitude - 78.9) < 0.05, "C6 fallback by 78.9 ms at 1.3 m/s")

# ┌── 4. OUTPUT: rendered values ────────────────────────────────────────────────
class ReleaseClaims:
    budget_str = fmt_length(round(budget_aisle.magnitude, 1) * millimeter, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    v_aisle_str = fmt_velocity(AISLE.v_aisle, unit=meter / second, precision=1)
    d_clear_str = fmt_length(AISLE.d_clear, unit=meter, precision=2)
    f_cmd_str = fmt_qty(f_cmd, newton, precision=0)
    x_remaining_str = fmt_length(round(x_remaining.magnitude, 2) * millimeter, unit=millimeter, precision=2)
    a_arm_str = fmt_acceleration(round(a_arm_needed.magnitude) * meter / second**2, unit=meter / second**2, precision=0)
    f_latch_limit_str = fmt_qty(AISLE.f_latch_limit, newton, precision=0)
    f_handover_str = fmt_qty(f_handover, newton, precision=1)
    v_handover_str = fmt_velocity(AISLE.v_handover, unit=meter / second, precision=2)
    f_contact_str = fmt_qty(AISLE.f_contact_criterion, newton, precision=0)
    m1_str = fmt_qty(RM.loaded_mass, kilogram, precision=0)
    t_renewal_to_onset_str = fmt_latency(t_renewal_to_onset, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    wcet_str = fmt_latency(AISLE.enforcer_wcet, unit=microsecond, precision=0)
    deadline_str = fmt_latency(AISLE.enforcer_deadline, unit=microsecond, precision=0)
    mu_min_str = fmt(round(mu_min, 3), precision=3)
    t_age_str = fmt_latency(AISLE.perception_age, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    t_timeout_str = fmt_latency(round(t_timeout.magnitude, 1) * millisecond, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
```

For the mobile manipulator's arm, ISO 10218-1 and ISO 10218-2 frame the robot and integration assessment; ISO/TS 15066 informs the assessed collaborative-contact case [@isots15066]. The `{python} ReleaseClaims.f_contact_str` handover criterion is a selected, site-specific design criterion, not a universal limit from that specification. The release argument must name the contacted body region, pressure, geometry, and measurement method before using a biomechanical value.

ISO 26262 and ISO 21448 address road-vehicle electrical/electronic safety and intended-function limitations, respectively [@iso26262; @iso21448]. Their fault-versus-performance distinction is useful here as an analogy, but neither supplies an ASIL D certificate for this machine. An independent permission path can bound learned proposals only where its sensor coverage, plant model, actuator authority, timing, and fallback are validated. A shared bus, power rail, or sensor can defeat that independence; fault analysis and stress tests must examine those paths. Unknown obstacles or contact mechanics absent from the safety model remain release exclusions or reasons for conservative separation, not automatically solved by a control barrier.

The claim-argument-evidence scorecard in @tbl-16-cae-scorecard states six claims and pairs each physical warrant with its adjudication on this book's evidence. Claim C3 shows the decision: an oil film can defeat braking traction, so nominal model accuracy cannot justify an unrestricted verdict. Claim C6 stands only on the fault records that test the four authority rules @sec-intervention-authority-log hands over (A1–A4).
